title: Evaluating a Deterministic Validator Plus Single‑Iteration Repair Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configurations
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment (N=300 paired intent→configuration tasks; preregistration id cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1; preregistration SHA-256 archived) to measure whether a minimal guarded pipeline—single‑shot LLM generation (declared model: gpt-5-mini) followed by a frozen deterministic configuration validator and at most one automated repair iteration—reduces first‑pass misconfiguration relative to plain single‑shot generation. Execution completed 600 episodes and used 301 model calls. Observed outcomes: baseline = 299/300 valid (99.667%); guarded = 300/300 valid (100.0%); paired counts n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; absolute paired difference = 0.0033333; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). The single permitted automated repair corrected the sole invalid baseline output (repair success 1/1; Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]). The preregistered planning assumption used for power calculations (planned baseline pass rate = 0.40) was contradicted by the observed near‑ceiling baseline, removing statistical headroom for the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction target. We report preregistered design choices, execution accounting, confirmatory statistics, artifact‑grounded diagnostics, and reproducibility primitives; all run artifacts and analysis outputs are archived in the execution manifest referenced in the Disclosure Statement.

sections.introduction: Bridging operator intent and device configuration is central to NetOps. Large language models (LLMs) can synthesize configuration artifacts from high‑level intent but their probabilistic outputs risk misordering, omissions, and unsafe commands. Recent literature therefore advocates guarded architectures that pair probabilistic generators with deterministic validators/simulators and bounded repair loops to form operational floor‑safety nets. Despite proposals and demos, there is a shortage of preregistered, artifact‑archived experiments that quantify how tightly bounded validator+repair pipelines change first‑pass misconfiguration rates under controlled sampling semantics. We implement a narrowly scoped, preregistered paired experiment asking: Can a minimal guarded pipeline—single shared LLM candidate, a frozen deterministic validator, and ≤1 automated repair iteration—reduce the first‑pass misconfiguration rate relative to plain single‑shot generation under paired sampling? Contributions: (1) a preregistered paired experiment with deterministic task seeds and archived per‑task artifacts; (2) confirmatory statistics and exact accounting drawn from archived artifacts; (3) artifact‑grounded diagnostics and post‑hoc sensitivity bounds tied to observed discordant counts; (4) practical, artifact‑traceable recommendations for future confirmatory NetOps evaluations.
sections.related_work: LLM applications for intent→configuration and NetOps have matured in demos and lab evaluations showing promising template synthesis yet also documenting typical failure modes (misordering, omission, overconfidence) that threaten operational safety [10.1002/nem.2313]. Cross‑domain work in medical QA and code repair shows verifier‑assisted and retrieval‑augmented strategies reduce factual errors and improve grounding, motivating guarded NetOps architectures [10.36227/techrxiv.176784505.56675782/v1, 10.2139/ssrn.6608518]. Deterministic network verification (header‑space and specification checking) provides algorithmic foundations for validators capable of static reachability and policy checks without live execution [10.1145/3098822.3098834]. Survey and governance analyses emphasize generate→verify→repair with auditability and human oversight as critical open engineering needs [10.6028/nist.ai.100-2e2023]. Our work executes a preregistered empirical test of a minimal realization of this design pattern and reports artifact‑grounded quantitative outcomes.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and hypotheses: The study was preregistered as cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1 (preregistration SHA-256 archived). Confirmatory hypotheses: H1 — the guarded pipeline reduces first‑pass misconfiguration rate by ≥50% (relative) versus single‑shot generation; H2 — one or fewer automated repair iterations recover ≥75% of initially invalid configurations. The preregistration explicitly assumed a planning baseline pass rate = 0.40 for power calculations; this assumption is reported here because it influenced sample‑size planning and interpretation.

Design and sampling: We used a paired within‑task design with a frozen deterministic seed list of 300 tasks. Each seed produced an intent and canonical reference configuration. For each seed the pipeline produced a single shared initial candidate: that shared candidate served as the baseline response and, for the guarded arm, as the input to the frozen deterministic validator and the possible repair adapter. Planned episodes = 600 (300 pairs), initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1, maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1. The shared‑candidate pairing was preregistered to emulate operational workflows that remediate a single proposed plan rather than comparing independent draws; this semantics increases within‑pair correlation and reduces informative discordance for paired tests.

Declared model and provider policy: The declared generation model in the execution contract was gpt-5-mini. Execution accounting in the archived manifest shows model_calls_used = 301 and maximum_model_calls = 600. Important disclosure about sampling: the archived model configuration records show that the model sampling temperature was unset (execution/model_configuration.json records "temperature": null; artifact SHA-256 = 1acce92558edeb13cd97b75817329d332afe4a36d01d566f1a26c61b132923fa). A null/unset temperature is not evidence of deterministic sampling (temperature=0); sampling determinism was therefore unspecified by configuration and nondeterministic sampling cannot be ruled out. This has inferential implications: generator variance across independent draws may differ if temperature had been fixed to 0, and our shared‑candidate semantics used a single initial draw per seed so those cross‑draw variance effects were intentionally controlled by design.

Validator, canonicalization, scoring, and repair adapter: The frozen deterministic validator canonicalized generated configurations to a normalized AST and applied explicit static checks derived from task payload policies (required sequences, must_be_down_for_fields, group constraints). Scoring used full intent‑constraint validation: success requires that the validator's normalized_configuration satisfy the task's required_sequence and expected_final_state and that no protected constraints are violated. Validator traces include parsed_command_count, required_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, violation_codes, and a boolean valid flag; these traces are archived and were used to trigger repair. The preregistered repair adapter executes a single targeted automated edit when violations are reported; repair prompts/responses and post‑repair validation are archived per episode.

Contamination and missingness: The preregistration included deterministic contamination detection via normalized‑AST equality and deterministic near‑duplicate thresholds; exact duplicates would be excluded and replaced from a reserve list. Missingness handling followed the preregistered policy: pairs were only dropped if both episodes failed ('complete_pair_primary'); one allowed retry for provider failures was recorded in the manifest. All exclusions, replacements, failed calls, and retries are recorded in the execution manifest.
sections.results:
Execution accounting (artifact‑derived): planned episodes = 600; completed episodes = 600; complete pairs analyzed = 300; model_calls_used = 301 (300 shared initial generations + 1 repair invocation). No provider failures or preregistered exclusions occurred. Primary outcomes (archived counts): baseline_success_count = 299/300 (99.667%); guarded_success_count = 300/300 (100.0%). Archival paired contingency: n11 = 299, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Confirmatory inferential outputs (preregistered analysis): exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; observed absolute paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 1/300 ≈ 0.0033333. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI for the absolute paired difference = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Repair outcomes (H2): the single allowed automated repair corrected the sole invalid baseline output (repair success 1/1; Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]).

Post‑hoc sensitivity bound and interpretive arithmetic: The observed discordant total (n10 + n01 = 1) imposes a hard limit on resolvable absolute paired differences equal to 1/300 ≈ 0.00333. Thus the preregistered target (≥50% relative reduction from an assumed baseline of 0.40 ≈ absolute +0.30) would have required on the order of 90 net discordant pairs favoring guarded outputs for N=300; the archived contingency demonstrates that this expectation was unattainable given the observed near‑ceiling baseline. Representative validator and repair traces for the corrected episode are archived and document the specific violation codes and the minimal edit applied to satisfy intent constraints.
sections.discussion:
Artifact‑anchored interpretation. The archived paired counts and validator traces directly constrain inference: with only one discordant pair the exact McNemar test must yield a non‑significant result (p = 1.00) and bootstrap CIs collapse to reflect near‑zero absolute improvements. This outcome is a direct, reproducible consequence of preregistered pairing semantics (shared_initial_candidate) and the high baseline pass rate.

Design lessons for future confirmatory NetOps studies: (1) Align task difficulty or perform adversarial augmentation to produce a nontrivial baseline failure prevalence or a preregistered discordant‑pair target commensurate with the planned effect size; (2) Explicitly preregister pairing semantics and repair budgets because they materially affect expected discordance and power; (3) When runtime semantics matter for deployment claims, include emulation/simulation stages and preregister how emulator outcomes map to success/failure. These recommendations are traceable to archived artifacts: task difficulty fields, validator violation codes, and the paired contingency table.

Construct and external validity caveats. Our validator executes deterministic static checks and canonicalization rather than device/emulator execution; therefore results are conditional on validator semantics and do not measure dynamic runtime consequences (control‑plane convergence or transient dataplane reachability). The synthetic task bank, constrained vendor templates, and single declared model (gpt-5-mini) limit generality across real production topologies and model families. Repair effectiveness (H2) is imprecisely estimated because only one initial failure occurred; larger counts of initial failures are required to estimate conditional repair success with precision.

Operational implication. When baseline misconfiguration is already rare, the operational value of a validator+bounded repair pipeline may be as a catastrophic‑risk mitigation floor rather than as a throughput enhancer. Organizations should therefore align evaluation goals (error‑reduction vs catastrophic‑risk mitigation) with task bank selection, pairing semantics, and whether emulation is necessary to claim runtime safety benefits.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired experiment (N=300 pairs) comparing single‑shot LLM generation (gpt-5-mini) to a guarded pipeline comprising a frozen deterministic validator and a single automated repair iteration. Baseline generation produced 299/300 valid outputs and the guarded pipeline produced 300/300 valid outputs; the sole initially invalid baseline configuration was corrected by the single permitted automated repair. The preregistered planning assumption (baseline pass rate = 0.40) was contradicted by the observed near‑ceiling baseline, removing statistical headroom for the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction target. We present artifact‑grounded diagnostics and concrete design recommendations—calibrate task difficulty or adversarially augment tasks to ensure sufficient initial failures, preregister pairing semantics and repair budgets, and include emulation when runtime guarantees are required. All raw outputs, validator traces, repair traces, the execution manifest, and analysis artifacts are archived and enumerated in the Disclosure Statement to permit reproduction of the reported counts and intervals.

A null/unset temperature in the archived configuration is not equivalent to temperature=0 (deterministic sampling); sampling determinism was therefore unspecified by configuration. This nondisclosure of deterministic sampling has inferential implications because generator variance across independent draws depends on sampling settings; our preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics intentionally used a single draw per seed to evaluate the validator+repair effect on a single proposed plan. The execution manifest and analysis artifacts are the authoritative sources for the numeric counts reported in this manuscript. limitations: Synthetic task bank and constrained vendor‑template scope limit external validity to broad production environments.
Single declared LLM (gpt-5-mini) and a single validator implementation restrict generality across model families and validator designs.

The preregistered power plan assumed a baseline pass rate = 0.40; the observed baseline (299/300) contradicted that assumption and removed headroom to detect the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction.
Sampling semantics (shared_initial_candidate) reused the same initial candidate across paired arms, increasing within‑pair correlation and reducing discordant pairs available to McNemar inference.

Validation used deterministic configuration/constraint checks rather than full dynamic emulation of runtime semantic effects; actual runtime consequences of configurations were not executed and remain unmeasured.

H2 repair‑success evidence is based on a single initially invalid case (1/1 → 100%), yielding a wide Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]; larger counts of initial failures are required to estimate repair effectiveness precisely.
